The ferry was old and cheap. The bridge would cost more than the town's whole yearly revenue, and the money would have to be borrowed from a banking house in Reval. The recorder, Petra Lund, left four pages of minutes that give the hour of adjournment and the tally but not the arguments; what the council actually weighed has had to be reconstructed from the letters its members wrote that summer.

In the ice-run of March 1801 the ferry rope had parted and three people drowned within sight of the town landing, and the memory of it sat in the chamber all spring. Lorens Falk, the engineer the council had hired in 1799, argued against the bridge, and argued from the same fact. Piers set in a channel that narrow would catch the floes each March, dam them, and push the water back over the lower streets. Safety, he told the members, was the reason to leave the river alone.

The chamber had been divided since 1791, and Falk's warning kept it divided. Twice the members split six and six, and twice Margit Aden, who held the chair and its casting vote, declined to use it and adjourned the session instead. On the third division the tally was six and six again. This time Aden cast, and cast for the bridge, saying only that the town could not be asked to wait through another winter for a crossing.

The town borrowed a second time and opened a fourth arch in 1814, after which the flooding stopped. The bridge Kirrholm wanted was the bridge Kirrholm got. The objection it had voted down was also correct, and the correction cost more in 1814 than it would have cost in 1802.

prompt: According to the passage, what did Rowe change on half of the 1,200 drops?
passage:
Every weekday for eleven weeks, Dr. Imani Rowe left unmarked envelopes on the paving stones of a busy transit plaza and waited to see what strangers would do. Each envelope held a blank card and nothing of value. A staffed lost-property kiosk stood about twenty metres away, and Rowe's team counted an envelope as returned only if it reached that counter within the hour. Field studies of this kind trade the tidiness of a laboratory for the messiness of real behaviour, and Rowe accepted the trade willingly. Across 1,200 drops, the plain envelopes came back 38 percent of the time.

Rowe's interest lay in a single change. On half of the drops, a first name and a short line of thanks were inked by hand across the envelope's corner, in what looked plainly like the loser's own handwriting. Under that condition returns climbed to 61 percent, a gap far larger than the weather, the hour, or the density of the crowd could account for. Rowe argued that the writing worked by making the loser particular: it is easy to step around an abstraction and hard to step around a person, and a name turns a dropped object into somebody's loss, even when the finder will never meet that somebody.

Dr. Tomas Vance, who studies pedestrian movement, was unconvinced. His objection was not that Rowe's numbers were wrong; he accepted every one of them. It was that writing on an envelope is also a signal about contents, since people label what matters to them, and that finders were answering an impression of worth rather than any particular person.

The two designed a joint follow-up for the next spring, nine hundred drops in the same plaza, arranged so that their explanations predicted different results. One arm kept the inked name. The other carried a stamped serial number and the words CONTAINS PAYMENT, impersonal but unmistakably about stakes. The stamped envelopes came back 62 percent of the time and the inked ones 61. Rowe published the revision herself and now calls the effect a judgement about worth.

Rowe has become careful with the word why. The plaza gave her a number that almost anyone could go and reproduce; what it never handed over, she says, was the reason underneath it.

A printed slip under the flap saying that most people who find one of these hand it in at the kiosk.
A first name and a short line of thanks inked by hand across the corner of the envelope.
A convex mirror clamped to the kiosk, angled so that a person lifting an envelope caught sight of their own face.
correct_answer: A first name and a short line of thanks inked by hand across the corner of the envelope.
explanation: The passage specifies "a first name and a short line of thanks were inked by hand across the envelope's corner."

Ferrow Bank is a low mound of turf and shell sand on the north shore of the Cluvie estuary, dry at spring tide and too small to interest anyone but the sheep that graze it. For eleven summers a team led by Dr. Ines Calvo has taken it apart a trowel-width at a time. Under a collapsed roof of driftwood they reached a floor of packed clay, and on the floor lay two dozen fired clay loom weights in a line where an upright loom had toppled, a scatter of spindle whorls, and, in a waterlogged dip beside them, a wad of unspun fleece still greasy to the touch.

The floor held charcoal as well, and charcoal can be dated. Twenty-six samples went to the laboratory at Ardnave. The results came back in one bundle. The dates are strung thinly across nearly four hundred years, and there is no gap anywhere in the sequence and no crowding either. Calvo takes this to mean that small parties came back to the mound for a few days at a time, generation after generation, rather than settling on it in any single stretch.

Professor Dermot Halloran, who has excavated four comparable mounds on the far shore, reads the same floor differently. The mound, he argues, was not a workshop at all but an ordinary dwelling; weaving gear turns up on the floor of every house he has dug on the far shore, six or eight weights at a time, and nobody calls those houses factories. The quantity here, he says, is a little larger and nothing else, and proves nothing about who worked there.

Calvo does not brush the objection aside. She says the question is one that a measurement can decide. Loom weights wear where the cords run over them. A specialist at Ardnave is measuring those grooves under a microscope against weights from houses of the same century. Cords rethreaded a few times a year cut shallow; cords rethreaded daily cut deep, and the two do not resemble each other. The results are not yet in.

Neither archaeologist expects the mound to be generous for much longer. The sea has already cut into its seaward side, and what the estuary takes it does not give back. Two summers remain in the excavation permit, and both will be spent in the strip nearest the water, where the waterlogged dip that preserved the fleece runs on into the eroding face; if more fibre survives in it, the range of wools and plant threads worked on the mound can at last be established.

Melting copper alloy in small clay pots and casting it.
Drying and sprouting barley in a stone bowl over heat.

For six seasons Ines Marchetti followed grey chatterbirds through the thorn scrub of the eastern Karoo, and for six seasons one habit refused to make sense. Chatterbirds keep a piercing two-note call for hawks alone; when it sounds, every bird within earshot drops flat or dives into cover, and nobody forages for a minute or more. Yet Marchetti's notebooks filled with hawkless alarms — three hundred and forty of them, by her own count, with nothing overhead but cloud.

Her first thought was ordinary error: a shadow, a startled dove, a bird jumping at nothing. But mistakes ought to be scattered evenly through a group, and these were not. Sixty-nine percent of the hawkless calls came from whichever bird had taken the sentinel perch above the group, the one spot from which the whole foraging party can be watched, and a sentinel has the least excuse for mistaking a shadow.

What followed the calls was just as lopsided. Marchetti filmed fifty-eight hawkless alarms at close range. In forty-one of them the caller dropped from its perch within seconds and carried off the item a startled neighbour had let fall — usually something bulky: a scorpion, a hairless mouse, a beetle grub too fat to swallow whole.

Correlation is not proof, so in her fifth season Marchetti set out to make the alarms happen. On alternate mornings she baited the feeding stations either with slivers of meat that go down in a gulp or with whole scorpions, which a bird must beat and dismember in the open. Marchetti now calls the hawkless alarm a lie told for a mouthful: a signal meaning hawk, given by a bird that eats when everyone else believes it. What she cannot explain is why the lie still works. A hundred and forty liars a season ought to have taught the flock to ignore the call, and it has not. Whether the callers hold the trick below some rate at which listeners would stop believing it is the question she means to answer next.

Chatterbirds keep a piercing two-note call for hawks alone; when it sounds, every bird within earshot drops flat or dives into cover, and nobody forages for a minute or more. Yet Marchetti's notebooks filled with hawkless alarms — three hundred and forty of them, by her own count, with nothing overhead but cloud.

Her first thought was ordinary error: a shadow, a startled dove, a bird jumping at nothing. But mistakes ought to be scattered evenly through a group, and these were not. Sixty-nine percent of the hawkless calls came from whichever bird had taken the sentinel perch above the group, the one spot from which the whole foraging party can be watched, and a sentinel has the least excuse for mistaking a shadow.

What followed the calls was just as lopsided. Marchetti filmed fifty-eight hawkless alarms at close range. In forty-one of them the caller dropped from its perch within seconds and carried off the item a startled neighbour had let fall — usually something bulky: a scorpion, a hairless mouse, a beetle grub too fat to swallow whole.

Correlation is not proof, so in her fifth season Marchetti set out to make the alarms happen. On alternate mornings she baited the feeding stations either with slivers of meat that go down in a gulp or with whole scorpions, which a bird must beat and dismember in the open. Hawkless alarms were five times more common on scorpion mornings, and on those mornings the caller finished the meal.

Marchetti now calls the hawkless alarm a lie told for a mouthful: a signal meaning hawk, given by a bird that eats when everyone else believes it. What she cannot explain is why the lie still works. A hundred and forty liars a season ought to have taught the flock to ignore the call, and it has not. Whether the callers hold the trick below some rate at which listeners would stop believing it is the question she means to answer next.
choices: That interrupted males resume the same display moments later at no cost.
That the calls are just as frequent in seasons when no young are being reared.
That callers routinely leave the dropped prey untouched rather than collecting it.
That scattered groups pull back together just as quickly when no call is given.
correct_answer: That callers routinely leave the dropped prey untouched rather than collecting it.
explanation: The conclusion rests on the caller being "a bird that eats when everyone else believes it."

prompt: According to the passage, what led Harbrook to enclose Coldwater Creek in 1911?
passage:
Coldwater Creek crossed Harbrook for as long as the city had a name, cutting a shallow meander through the flats east of the courthouse. In 1911 the council voted to put it underground.

The reason was waste. The state ordinance of 1908 had ordered Harbrook to carry its sewage below the town landing, and the creek's bed was by far the cheapest line to the river. Enclosing the channel, the council's resolution said, would "make of the creek a conduit fit for the city's discharge."

The work took nineteen months. Crews laid a barrel of hard-fired brick, four rings thick and nine feet across, for one and a quarter miles, and backfilled the old channel with cinders from the gasworks. The creek did not stop running; it stopped being visible. Within a decade the city's maps no longer drew it, and the street grid crossed the old meander as though the ground there had always been flat. Harbrook's public works ledger names the barrel only twice between 1930 and 1998, each time as a line item for clearing a grate.

The silence ended in 2019, when the city engineer, Nadia Ferrar, sent a camera crawler the length of the barrel — the first full inspection on record.

The barrel itself was strong. Ferrar's crawler found the brick rings sound along nearly their whole length, and the bore wide enough for twice the flow it held. What it held was the difficulty. Eleven of the city's sewer laterals still emptied into it, and in any rain the barrel ran as one mixed stream to the river, where Ferrar's samplers logged forty-one discharge events in a single year. The pipe was doing its 1911 job perfectly, and its 1911 job was the thing now objected to.

Ferrar's report circulated for four years. Four factions formed in the council chamber: one for repair, one for enlargement, one for removal, one for waiting, each with a cost estimate and a constituency.

In June 2023 they chose waiting: $6.9 million for five years of continuous monitoring, annual dredging and a full separation study, with no lining, tunnel or excavation authorized until it reports. The barrel would go on carrying what it carries — which was, after all, the only thing the city had so far settled.
choices: An outbreak of typhoid in 1909, traced to privy drainage entering the creek, which had killed thirty-one people on the flats.
A state ordinance in 1908 requiring the city to carry its sewage below the town landing, for which the creek bed was cheapest.
A rail yard's outright purchase of the meander in 1910, which needed forty acres of level ground before it could lay sidings.
A flood in 1907 that stood four feet deep on the flats for two days and backed water into three hundred houses.
correct_answer: A state ordinance in 1908 requiring the city to carry its sewage below the town landing, for which the creek bed was cheapest.
explanation: The passage states that "the state ordinance of 1908 had ordered Harbrook to carry its sewage below the town landing, and the creek's bed was by far the cheapest line to the river."
